articles.title: Xbox Wants to Eventually Reach More Than a Billion People Each Day, Asha Sharma Tells Staff the Target Is to Get Halfway There by 2030
articles.summary: Xbox boss Asha Sharma has told staff that by 2030, Microsoft's gaming business should hit the halfway point of its ambitious target of reaching more than a billion people each day.
articles.body:
Xbox boss Asha Sharma has told staff that by 2030, Microsoft's gaming business should hit the halfway point of its ambitious target of reaching more than a billion people each day.

CNBC reported that Sharma’s memo, which followed hot on the heels of difficult financial results for Microsoft’s gaming business , set out plans for revenue growth in the 2028 and 2029 fiscal years.

Earlier this month, Sharma cut 1,600 Xbox staff , with another 1,600 to go during the rest of this financial year. Four studios are out the door, with another on its way. The restructure will see a doubling down on big Xbox-owned video game franchises, such as Fallout, a significant investment in Minecraft, and a push for a more casual audience via the likes of Candy Crush.

Announcing the restructure, Sharma said she wanted Xbox to be “one of the few companies that entertains more than a billion people each day and gives everyone the opportunity to create and connect.” It was a somewhat improbable target that drew a healthy dose of scepticism from some quarters, but Sharma doubled down:

“I know we can achieve this goal,” she insisted. “Xbox has many of the most beloved franchises in entertainment history, talented studios around the world, and we will return to growth in 2027."

In this latest memo, Sharma went into more detail on this growth plan. In it, she said that her goal is for Xbox to be halfway towards that billion figure by 2030 — so, in four years time, Xbox will have half a billion people engaging with its gaming business each day.

“By FY30, our ambition is to be halfway to our long-term daily-player goal with sustained double-digit growth in players and engagement and industry leading margins,” she said.

To put the challenge into perspective, Sharma said Xbox currently has “more than 100 million people every day.” Xbox revenue declined 10% for the quarter ending June 30. When comparing the entire 2026 fiscal year to the 2025 fiscal year, Xbox revenue decreased by 7%, or around $1.7 billion. Xbox ended the financial year with a 3% internal margin (Sony operates at an around 10% margin, Nintendo 16%).

How will Xbox achieve this accelerated growth? “We will build long-term plans for our biggest franchises across film, television, consumer products, sponsorship, live experiences, and form new partnerships globally, including China,” Sharma wrote.

Xbox has three franchises that generate more than $1 billion annually — they’re thought to be Call of Duty, Minecraft, and Candy Crush. To reach its ambitious growth targets, Microsoft will need all three to grow further, while also growing other franchises, such as Fallout and Halo.

Then there’s the question of the next-generation console, Project Helix. There is talk of it potentially costing north of $1,000 as the RAMpocalypse continues to bite. Will console sales collapse as they become even more premium gaming devices than they already are?

Reacting to Xbox's tough financials in a tweet , Sharma said the company's recovery will take time, but it expects results in the next 12 months.

"In FY26, over 200 million new players came to Xbox and our games, but our business did not grow with our audience," Sharma said. "We need to close that gap by investing in what players value. That will take time, but we expect to return to growth by the end of FY27."

Microsoft boss Satya Nadella also touched on Xbox in a conference call with investors, saying: "When it comes to Xbox, we are making the necessary decisions required across our content portfolio, platform, and operations to reset the business for long term growth.

"We have the best IP in the industry, and talented studios around the world, and believe we can bring these strengths together and expect to return the business to growth in fiscal 2027."

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: 'Final Nail in the Coffin': Xbox Price Rises Revealed, Leaving Fans Stunned as Series X/S Spike By More Than a Third in Europe
articles.summary: Microsoft has increased the price of its consoles by more than a third in Europe, leaving fans stunned at how much an Xbox Series X/S now costs.
articles.body:
Microsoft has increased the price of its consoles by more than a third in Europe, leaving fans stunned at how much an Xbox Series X/S now costs.

While these price rises are not a surprise — Microsoft announced they were coming back in June — the exact pricing for Xbox Series X and S in mainland Europe and the UK remained under wraps until now.

In the U.S., Microsoft previously stated that the 512GB Series S would rise by $100, while 1TB Series models would rise by $150 — increases that equate to around £74 and £111. The 2TB model will be discontinued completely, meanwhile — presumably because it would have become too expensive to be worthwhile making.

But in the UK and mainland Europe, the actual price rises in pounds and euros are much steeper. The 512GB Series S has jumped from £299 to £429, an increase of £130, while its 1TB model has increased from £349 to £519, a leap of £170.

Worse still are the increases for Series X models, with the 1TB Digital up from £449 to £619 (£170), but the 1TB Disc model up from £449 to £669 — whopping 48% increase, and £220 difference.

Fans have slammed the huge changes, which are far higher than expected. "Final nail in the coffin," wrote one user on the video game forum ResetEra . "Great strategy, that'll definitely lead to more sales," said another. "There is no way in 2026 I would be paying nearly £700 for a Series X with a disc drive," wrote a third.

"Still trying to process how a console that was sold for €499 almost six years ago is now €799," noted another fan. "The Series S 1TB is now €100 more expensive than the Series X at launch. This is just mindblowing."

Xbox Series S (512GB) – $499.99 (was $399.99)

Xbox Series S (1TB) – $599.99 (was $449.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Digital) – $749.99 (was $599.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Disc) – $799.99 (was $649.99)

Xbox Series S (512GB) – £429.99 (was £299.99)

Xbox Series S (1TB) – £519.99 (was £349.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Digital) – £619.99 (was £449.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Disc) – £669.99 (was £499.99)

Xbox Series S (512GB) – €499.99 (was €349.99)

Xbox Series S (1TB) – €599.99 (was €399.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Digital) – €749.99 (was €549.99)

Xbox Series X (1TB, Disc) – €799.99 (was €599.99)

Back in June, Microsoft blamed this latest set of price rises as the result of console storage and memory prices having "increased by more than 2.5x," with another "doubling by the fall of 2027" expected.

"The entire consumer electronics industry is struggling with the current components crisis, but the effects are particularly hard on consoles," Microsoft wrote. Unlike phones, computers, speakers, and other consumer devices, consoles are typically not sold at a profit, but instead for less than they cost to make."

The anouncement of the Xbox console price rises comes ahead of the release of GTA 6 in November, which is expected to increase demand for PS5 and Xbox Series X and S significantly. However, there are concerns that neither Sony nor Microsoft will be able to meet the demand caused by the release of GTA 6, with the AI boom making it particularly hard for hardware manufacturers not only to source components, but to release products at affordable prices.

Earlier this year, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said the spiralling cost of new and existing consoles would require "radically different business models" over the coming generation. She added that the industry had "reached a point where it will be hard to imagine" mass audiences still being able to afford "thousands of dollars" for a new console generation.

The current PS5 and Xbox Series X and S generation of consoles have seen price increases rather than cost savings. Sony itself raised the price of PS5 consoles back in March , blaming "continued pressures in the global economic landscape." Nintendo has also not been immune, and recently acknowledged it would up the price of Switch 2, just over a year after its arrival. And Valve has bemoaned its struggle to release Steam Machine at the price it had initially hoped , instead having to go for an eye-watering $1,049.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Ted Lasso Sets the Stage for a Soft Reboot With a Kansas City-Set Season 4 Premiere
articles.summary: Ted Lasso Season 4 premiere review: Ted returns with an engaging Kansas City-set season premiere that catches us up with a few key characters, setting the stage for the show’s new soft reboot approach following a three-year absence.
articles.body:
Ted Lasso Season 4 debuts August 5 on Apple TV .

Three years after a Season 3 finale that sure did feel like a series finale at the time, Ted Lasso is back for a fourth season after all. In the modern streaming world, it’s become far too typical for a three-year gap between seasons to become something of a norm. At least Ted Lasso is accounting for this prolonged break in a bigger way, with a semi-reboot approach that feels more akin to a show being revived 10-15 years later rather than one we last saw the same year Oppenheimer was in movie theaters.

The third season ended with Ted (Jason Sudeikis) returning home to America and realizing it was time to stop being the semi-deadbeat dad he’d become, given his young son was back in Kansas City while Ted had been overseas coaching AFC Richmond. Season 4’s premiere is notable, because it’s actually entirely set in Kansas City. Ted is surprised when Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), Leslie (Jeremy Swift), and Keeley (Juno Temple) show up on his doorstep, hoping to recruit him to return to London to coach the new AFC Richmond women’s division team.

The premiere was shot on location in Kansas City, giving it a markedly different visual landscape than your typical Ted Lasso episode, and it makes the most of it. And there’s plenty of comic mileage drawn from making Rebecca, Leslie, and Keeley the fish out of water for once, as they take in these new sights and sounds. The cast all slip very comfortably back into their characters, whether it be the sweet and funny sisterly connection Waddingham and Temple exude, or the lovably dorky demeanor of Swift’s Leslie.

As for the title character, series co-creator and EP Sudeikis still wears the smile and stache of Ted like he was born for it. Ted’s gotten through the mental health issues that plagued him early on, but we find him at a restless point of his life, working as an assistant manager at a supermarket. He’s still maintaining his usual sunny disposition, but clearly without a true sense of fulfillment. Of course, there’s not a lot of dramatic tension as to whether he’ll accept the offer to coach again — there’s a whole season’s worth of episodes to fill, and we’ve seen the trailers — but the premiere does a solid job of showing how Ted gets to the point where he can admit that’s what he wants to do.

Pushing things on the credibility side though is how the premiere deals with the fact that Ted not only wouldn’t want to leave his son Henry (now played by Grant Feely) again, but wouldn’t want to ask to separate Henry from his mother, Ted’s ex-wife Michelle (Andrea Anders). The solution feels far too easy and convenient, awkwardly handwaving what would likely be a very difficult conversation in real life.

Given the nature of the premiere and how focused it is — no other series regulars appear beyond the four mentioned above, and we never actually see London — it’s hard to be sure how much it will reflect the remainder of the season. But the approach it takes is promising as far as its willingness to lock in on just a few characters and interconnected situations.

While Ted Lasso never lost its kindhearted center, Season 3 was notably overindulgent and often felt lacking in form after EP/co-creator Bill Lawrence stepped back as showrunner. This was demonstrated by its incredibly overlong episode runtimes, which frequently hit a full hour or more in the midst of a show that began with half-hour installments. The amount of subplots and side stories got out of control to the point that we somehow were following the inner workings of two different restaurants at one point on a series that was meant to be about a soccer team.

As we prep to meet AFC Richmond's women's team, it’s definitely going to be odd adjusting to saying goodbye to the entire team we’ve spent the last three seasons invested in, and I do worry that it will feel even more difficult to move on thanks to the show still being set in the same location as before with most of the same support staff in place. It likely would have been an easier transition to send Ted and a few key players to an all new part of the world for a cleaner break from what came before, but even as we prep for these big changes, the premiere does give hope that Sudeikis and new co-showrunner Jack Burditt have learned that less can be more. Ted Lasso needed to feel more reined in again… albeit with a 47-minute runtime. Hey, that’s still short by Season 3’s standards! And while we have yet to meet the new team, the prospect of returning to the Season 1 feel of Ted and his team getting to know each other and once more starting from a true underdog perspective is a welcome one.

articles.title: Xbox Console Updates Adding New Capture and Achievement Features
articles.summary: Xbox has announced another set of new console features, which will begin rolling out to some users from today.
articles.body:
Xbox has announced another set of new console features, which will begin rolling out to some users from today.

As ever, these new features will begin being tested by Xbox Insiders in the Alpha Skip-Ahead ring, before slowing becoming available to all Xbox owners over the coming weeks.

The biggest addition here looks to be the ability to include party chat audio within gameplay captures, so you can fully remember a particular gaming moment and the reactions that came along with it. This feature has been designed so that individual party members can choose whether their audio can be captured, and only will be after players manually opt in.

Achievement hunters will likely celebrate to see an expanded set of options for tracking your progress, with your cheevo list now sortable by Last Played, Completion Percentage, Gamerscore Earned, Number of Achievements Unlocked, and more. And yes, you can sort these categories in ascending or descending order, allowing you to highlight where you're close to the full 1000G, or ready to start unlocking a new game's achievements from the off.

Next up, cloud saves. Players will be able to view and restore previous cloud save versions in supported games, starting with Forza Horizon 6, allowing you to recover an older progress point if necessary. If you ever experience a corrupted save (or want to go back and replay part of a game differently), this option should help you out.

And finally, Xbox is expanding your game wishlist — allowing you to add up to 1,000 titles. That should be enough, surely?

Today's updates come just days after Microsoft's latest set of Xbox console price rises have kicked in , raising the cost of some Xbox Series X and S models by up to $150 in the U.S., and up to an additional £220 in the U.K.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Xbox Is Planning Its Own Version of the Platinum Trophy
articles.summary: Xbox achievement hunters have something to look forward to this year, as the platform is planning its own take on the platinum trophy.
articles.body:
Xbox achievement hunters have something to look forward to this year, as the platform is planning its own take on the platinum trophy.

When the Xbox 360 launched in 2005, it came with a new feature known as achievements. If you do something cool in the game or make progress in the story, you'll be rewarded with points and an achievement to display on your profile. It was a really smart way to keep players engaged, push them to do things they might otherwise avoid, and increase competition. While Xbox wasn't the first company in gaming to utilize a feature like this, it absolutely popularized it, and it led to competitors like PlayStation mimicking the idea with trophies.

The trophy model is nearly identical to achievements, but the only difference is that you get a special reward when you get all the trophies in a PlayStation game: the lucrative platinum trophy. It's the end-all, be-all for completionists and now, Xbox is trying to emulate that. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has confirmed that, along with other updates to achievements , the team is looking to implement some kind of platinum trophy equivalent on Xbox later this year.

No details were provided on what that will look like, but it is exciting nevertheless. Typically, the average game's achievements cap out at 1,000 gamerscore, unless it's a collection of games or there's DLC. It's unclear if this new completionist achievement will add more gamerscore or be standalone as a recognition for your efforts.

This is something the Xbox community has wanted for a while, so it's great to see Microsoft implementing this level of feedback. It would be one of the biggest changes and additions to the Xbox achievement system since its introduction 21 years ago. It's unclear if this will retroactively apply to other games or if it will only be possible in new games, but it should be really cool regardless.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Nintendo Switch 2 Console Images Reportedly Leak
articles.summary: Leaked images of a The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Nintendo Switch 2 console and Pro Controller appear to be circulating online.
articles.body:
Leaked images of a The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Nintendo Switch 2 console and Pro Controller appear to be circulating online.

Photos of the unannounced Nintendo hardware were posted to X/Twitter today by Necro Felipe, the owner of well-known Brazilian gaming site Universo Nintendo, who stated that, per his sources, the designs were legitimate. IGN has contacted Nintendo for comment.

The images show a Switch 2 dock with golden Triforce design printed on one side, and a Switch 2 console with black/teal Joy-Con controllers, each also adorned with Triforce patterns.

VAZA encarte do Nintendo Switch 2 temático de Zelda (40 Anos) pic.twitter.com/4cmTceyxeb — 'Necro' Felipe #UnivNintendo (@necrolipe) August 11, 2026

VAZA encarte do Nintendo Switch 2 temático de Zelda (40 Anos) pic.twitter.com/4cmTceyxeb

A matching Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller: The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition mirrors the black/teal coloring for its base, with a golden central Triforce design and gold shoulder buttons and triggers.

Mais ângulos (e encartes) do encarte para o Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller - The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition https://t.co/nRJmlPwxWw pic.twitter.com/RiCOSEiZto — 'Necro' Felipe #UnivNintendo (@necrolipe) August 11, 2026

Mais ângulos (e encartes) do encarte para o Nintendo Switch 2 Pro Controller - The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition https://t.co/nRJmlPwxWw pic.twitter.com/RiCOSEiZto

An unrevealed Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary logo can be seen on packaging for both items, featuring a small NES-era Link icon. It'll be interesting to see where else this logo pops up, and how Nintendo markets its big Zelda anniversary.

To date, Nintendo has not marked Zelda's 40th anniversary year — and the actual date that the first Zelda game launched on NES has now come and gone. But there are still several months of 2026 left, and the company has now confirmed it will release its The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 remake before the year ends.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Trailer June 2026 Nintendo Direct - Screenshots

Nintendo fans expect a big Zelda 40th anniversary push soon, with more details of that Ocarina remake, the official reveal of this hardware, and a first trailer for the franchise's live-action movie that's set to debut on April 30, 2027. Perhaps we'll see all of this revealed in an upcoming Nintendo Direct?

Last week, various pieces of casting information also leaked , adding to the sense that leaks are happening now as Nintendo begins readying a big reveal. The late, great Sam Neil was reported to be part of the film's cast, alongside the previously leaked Dichen Lachen (Succession) as Impa, Uli Latukefu as Ganondorf, plus Yvonne Strahovski and Lydia Peckham in unknown roles.

Benjamin Evan Ainsworth, the young House of the Dragon star set to play Link, has recently offered his first thoughts on playing the Nintendo legend , meanwhile.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 2 – The Legacy Review
articles.summary: Grand Theft Auto 2 boasts a number of noticeable technical improvements over the original and feels far better to play, but I'm glad its odd and unrecognisable setting was a one-time experiment.
articles.body:
Over the next few months, I’m going to be taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t carry IGN’s typical score out of 10, because it really wouldn’t be at all fair to simply pick apart old games published multiple hardware generations ago and make them sweat under the harsher standards of 2026. What we will be doing, however, is re-examining what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release, digging into what they achieved and the legacies they established, and rediscovering how much fun each of them remain today. We’ll also be identifying both the parts of the GTA experience that have seen the most evolution and growth, as well as the parts that remain fascinating, commendable, and timelessly impressive. At the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly sit in my long-term love for this series.

Grand Theft Auto 2 arrived right at the tail end of the 20th century, sticking with the same brand of top-down turmoil that previously propelled its predecessor to great success. It’s a noticeable refinement of the original in some fundamental ways – slightly more forgiving thanks to the ability to save, and also a bit smoother to drive around in. It didn’t, however, replace its antiquated, tank-like on-foot controls for something that better exploited the dual-analogue controllers that had rapidly reinvented the status quo in the late ’90s. What it did shed was the original GTA’s recognisable, contemporary setting. It instead opted to set its action at an unspecified point in the near future, in a stylised, retro-futuristic backdrop called Anywhere City, USA – a place overrun by gangs, ruled by a megacorporation, and featuring the highest rate of Elvis Presley’s per capita this side of Graceland. Did it work? Well, the answer – unlike Anywhere City’s proliferation of Elvis impersonators – requires a little more conversation.

GTA 2 immediately comes off as a game with a bit of an identity crisis. Even if you ignore the fact that it sports a totally different look and vibe to the original, it also completely clashes with its own box art, and even its own intro movie – which features contemporaneous ’90s cars and an obvious New York setting. At the time of its release, I actually bounced off GTA 2 rather quickly, and this was absolutely a major reason. As soon as it began it just felt like an entirely unrelated product to everything that had come before – up to and including the tone-setting FMV intro it just served me. That’s a really weird problem to have. As a result, I don’t feel like I stuck around anywhere near long enough back in 1999 to get a feel for how much slicker it actually is to play.

Despite the fact it costs in-game currency to use, the addition of a save function represents a clear improvement over the original. Just head to the nearest church, and the good lord above will remember your progress for you. Jesus indeed saves in Anywhere City, albeit for a fee. Straight away GTA 2 appears a little more aware it’s a PC and home console product. By the late ’90s, hefty, mission-oriented action games had largely moved on from the ruthless arcade philosophy of starting from scratch every session with a tiny set of lives. Developer DMA Design adjusted its format accordingly, albeit only slightly. That is, GTA 2 retains score-based progression, still operates with strictly limited lives, and is hard as hell – but saving is nonetheless a crutch the original did not have.

A newly added health bar addresses another major frustration from the original GTA. If you’re trying to avoid cheating just to get through the missions, the boosted health is an even more useful fix than saving. Health in GTA 2 works on a 10-point scale (with five hearts that can be halved). This is in stark contrast to the first GTA, which essentially operates with your character on his or her final sliver of life at all times – where you’re instantly wasted after sustaining just a single hit. The tank controls make dodging incoming fire hideously difficult in both games, but the challenge is at least tempered here by the very sensible addition of that extra padding. It doesn’t make it easy, by any means, but it’s certainly less annoying.

The improvements don’t stop there. GTA 2’s camera is considerably less janky and, while it still shimmies around a little as you drive, it does a way better job of tracking cars smoothly. Cars also self-straighten when blazing along the streets, so it’s far less finicky to line up within a lane – or indeed change lanes – with less furious tapping of the d-pad.

There are also far fewer obstacles for cars to get hung up on than there were in the original. With the top-down perspective, it can be challenging to tell what objects are rooted into the ground and will cause a crash, because depth can be a difficult thing to effectively communicate from directly above. GTA 2 skirts this by having skinny things like light poles not even register to cars at all. It's not a particularly realistic approach, but it cuts down on the constant collisions which bogged down the pace of the original.

Cars can now be fitted out with weapons and gadgets, like machine guns, mines, and oil slick traps, and the amount of handheld weapons has been more than doubled. GTA 2 adds tossable explosives like grenades and Molotovs, a suppressed SMG that won’t alert other nearby NPCs, a shotgun for more devastating close quarters damage, dual pistols to dial up the John Woo factor, and a futuristic electro gun that will saute suckers into skeletons. The electro gun is particularly nifty considering it can lock onto multiple targets at once, but a mild auto-aim function (an assist sorely missed in GTA 1) makes for less frustrating combat all around, regardless of what weapon you’re using.

Despite the more polished gameplay, GTA 2 still leaves me indifferent in a number of ways. I know that merging the aesthetic of ’40s and ’50s vehicles with a crime-ridden, near-future corporate dystopia is a stylistic choice, but it just doesn’t really grab me. It’s not that I don’t find this era of automotive history interesting – I love skidding around in games like Mafia and LA Noire – but they just look silly in this setting and don’t sync with it at all.

It’s really easy to tell cars apart in the original GTA, because they resemble real cars and they all look quite distinct. In GTA 2, there are more than 60 different vehicles, but there are far too many that look too similar to each other – and none that really resemble anything particularly iconic. They just look like caricatures of cars, and I vastly prefer the realism of the original GTA’s vehicles.

I also prefer the original’s maps over the three districts of Anywhere City (the Downtown Sector, the Residential Sector, and the Industrial Sector). Now, GTA 2 boasts sharper graphics than its slightly murkier predecessor, and the effect of this cleaner image arguably makes it the more timeless-looking of the two. On PC there are even day and night versions of each area. However, with the possible exception of the Residential Sector (which is the most varied), there’s a plainness to Anywhere City that I don’t think the cities in the original GTA shared.

I do enjoy how much more alive and dangerous Anywhere City feels – with muggers, carjackers, and gang members scurrying the sidewalks everywhere as an omnipresent threat. However, I don’t think it has the charm of Liberty City, San Andreas, or Vice City – as primitive as their renditions were by modern standards.

I’m willing to concede my preference here may simply be because the amount of time I sunk into those maps dwarfs the moments I’ve spent in Anywhere City, but there is also something bigger at play. The 3,500 pound, 350-horsepower elephant in the room here is Driver, which was released on PlayStation in European territories about five months before GTA 2, in June 1999. Now, the original Driver has no on-foot component – so it’s not an entirely like-for-like comparison – but it is a fully 3D, open-world car chase classic that rapidly cemented itself as more or less my favourite game of all time at that moment. I’d seen the future, and GTA 2 couldn’t lure me back.

The dawn of 3D action-driving games was upon us. Prior to Driver we’d already seen Midtown Madness on PC, from future Midnight Club, Smuggler’s Run, and Red Dead Redemption developers Angel Studios. Following Driver came Mucky Foot’s ambitious but janky Urban Chaos in late 1999 on PC and early 2000 on PlayStation, which boasted a primitive brand of driving and third-person action. A PlayStation-exclusive Driver sequel followed in late 2000, where you could exit cars to steal another. June 2001’s World’s Scariest Police Chases sank with little trace after arriving on PS1 after the PS2 had launched, but it was actually a surprisingly decent open-world driving game of its own considering the totally outmoded hardware it was running on.

Any way you slice it, GTA 2 was a buck late and a dimension short to be a part of the first wave of 3D action-driving games.

Of course, the series wouldn’t be the bridesmaid for long – but that’s a discussion for next time.

Playing Grand Theft Auto 2 again in 2026, I’ve definitely found myself with a stronger appreciation for its technical improvements over the original. Certainly much greater than I gave it credit for back as a teenager in 1999. The driving is better, the shooting is better – and those are important and welcome gains. However, I just cannot muster any true enthusiasm for its retro-futuristic setting. I don’t know that I’d go so far as to call it aggravating but, in the words of the king of rock and roll, it just ain’t satisfactioning me.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: This 50-Hour Fantasy Audiobook Is the Best Possible Use of an Audible Free Trial
articles.summary: The Wandering Inn is considered to be a part of the LitRPG genre, which is very similar to Dungeon Crawler Carl, and I can't recommend it enough.
articles.body:
There are a lot of great fantasy audiobooks out there, but if you're looking to make the most of an Audible free trial, there's only one I recommend. The Wandering Inn series is one of my absolute favorites of the past decade and it has the added benefit of having an unusually lengthy first audiobook. At nearly 50 hours of listening time, it's the best possible bang for your buck.

The Wandering Inn is considered to be a part of the LitRPG genre , which is very similar to Dungeon Crawler Carl . At its heart, however, the story fits very snugly within traditional fantasy. There's magic, dragons, goblins, and even the occasional ogre. The audiobooks feature terrific narration from Andrea Parsneau and are definitely worth your time.

The average length of most audiobooks is between 10 and 12 hours long, so why is The Wandering Inn almost 50 hours long? The answer lies in the nature of how the LitRPG genre got its start. Many of the best stories were originally published as web serials first before being adapted into other forms. The Wandering Inn in particular has an extremely lengthy intro into the series that was never intended to be contained within a single audiobook. The series has only recently received a paperback release and has had to split this first book into two separate parts. Surprisingly, the second audiobook entry is actually even longer at just over 61 hours.

I had a chance to interview the author of the series earlier this year and they discussed the move from web serial to audiobook: "I believe I was around Volume 4 when I received an email in my inbox from Podium asking if I was interested in an audiobook deal. I had turned down every single offer before that, but I had just watched The Martian in movie theatres and I thought that I had to give the audiobook company that published The Martian a chance," said Pirateaba. "All of that was luck, and many amazing things like Andrea Parsneau becoming the first narrator of the audiobook were all due to chance."

If you're new to audiobooks, there's an Audible free trial worth checking out. Audible launched its new Standard subscription plan earlier this year that gets you your first audiobook for free. There are a ton of incredible audiobooks to access as your first free listen, but if you want the most bang for your buck, I can't recommend The Wandering Inn enough. 50 hours of listening time should last you a full month and it's only $8.99 per month after that if you want to continue the series.

Jacob Kienlen is a Senior Audience Development Strategist and Writer for IGN. Born and raised in Portland, Oregon, he has considered the Northwest his home for his entire life. With a bachelor's degree in communication and 10 years of professional writing experience, his expertise is spread across a variety of different pop culture topics -- from TV series to books and the latest LEGO sets..

articles.title: Heroes Star Hayden Panettiere Dies at 36
articles.summary: The former child actor’s entertainment career spanned three decades.
articles.body:
American actress Hayden Panettiere has died at 36, reports ABC News.

“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden,” reads a statement provided by her representative. “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her – and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”

Further details regarding Panettiere’s death have not been made available at this time.

Widely known for her TV roles as Claire Bennet on the series Heroes and Juliette Barnes on Nashville, Panettiere’s entertainment career began on TV back in the mid ’90s. She made her feature film debut at just nine years old as the voice of Princess Dot in 1998’s A Bug’s Life and went on to appear in many other films, including Remember the Titans, Raising Helen, the Scream franchise, and I Love You, Beth Cooper.

Panettiere was also a voice actor in a number of Kingdom Hearts games, and starred as Samantha Giddings in PlayStation’s Until Dawn.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team.

articles.title: Halloween: The Game Will Actually Be Available in New Zealand After All
articles.summary: Developer IllFonic alters course, and the game will now be made available digitally for NZ.
articles.body:
In the wake of Halloween: The Game being refused classification in Australia last week, and the subsequent confirmation that the game would not be available in Australia and New Zealand as a result , IGN reached out to IllFonic to clarify why the New Zealand release was affected. For example, Hotline Miami 2 is a game that was refused classification in Australia (and has remained so, unlike most high-profile RC cases, where developers typically make small changes to skirt the country’s classification guidelines). However, while Hotline Miami 2 is not available on storefronts in Australia, it is still very much available digitally in New Zealand . So the news of Halloween: The Game needing to be unavailable in New Zealand didn’t quite add up.

We’re yet to receive a response from IllFonic, but the studio has since announced that Halloween: The Game will be available in New Zealand after all , albeit in digital format only.

“We are extremely thrilled to announce that after receiving additional guidance from the OFLC, Office of Film and Literature Classification in New Zealand, Halloween: The Game will be available for sale digitally in the territory,” the studio published in a statement on social media.

“When we partnered with physical distributors (as we do not handle) to sell packaged goods in Australia and New Zealand, we learned that the ACB [the Australian Classification Board] rating (used for physical) took precedence of the IARC rating (used for digital). When ACB [sic] refused us a rating, it meant the removal of both physical and digital versions in those territories.”

Classification decisions made by the Australian Classification Board (ACB) itself do override automated decisions applied by the International Age Rating Coalition (IARC) global rating tool (which spits out PEGI, ESRB, ACB, etc. ratings from a single, free online questionnaire). However, ‘refused classification’ (RC) determinations made by the Australian Classification Board are not automatically mirrored in NZ.

New Zealand’s classification system regarding video games is somewhat idiosyncratic. While the NZ classification system does, in fact, utilise some Australian and UK classification decisions as a shortcut to make its own classifications, this is applicable to unrestricted content. Content that has been specifically age-restricted in Australia or the UK, refused classification in Australia, or banned in the UK must otherwise be formally classified by NZ’s Office of Film and Literature Classification. In NZ, games are actually expressly exempt from labelling requirements and are not required to be submitted for local classification unless likely to be awarded an age-restricted rating – or have already been given an age-restricted rating (or RC/banned) in Australia or the UK. So, to be available on physical formats in NZ, Halloween: The Game was always going to need to be submitted to the NZ OFLC, because games with restricted content must be classified by the OFLC and carry a NZ label in order to be sold. No rating for Halloween: The Game appears in the NZ Register of Classification Decisions, making a physical release in NZ currently impossible, even if it had been successfully classified in Australia.

However, NZ’s Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 only really covers physical formats, which means games sold digitally don’t necessarily always have NZ classifications displayed.

As for Halloween: The Game’s RC status in Australia, which IllFonic’s claims it has made “every effort” to work past, IGN has specifically asked the developer if there is a reason the game can’t be altered to suit the classification guidelines. As the Australian Classification Board explained, “Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player.” While games can feature drug use in Australia, they can’t offer gameplay rewards or incentives. If they do, the Classification Board is obligated to give the game a ‘Refused Classification’ determination.

As we noted to IllFonic, developers typically skirt this one particular guideline in Australia with semantics. For instance, in 2013 State of Decay developer Undead Labs simply renamed the drugs in the game to vitamins in Australia to hurdle this whole issue. If the RC determination is indeed related to smoking marijuana as a perk to highlight the location of Michael Myers on the map, we’ve asked IllFonic for clarification on whether it’s been considered that this could just be referred to and regarded as tobacco in Australia.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.summary:

articles.title: Avengers: Doomsday Star Sebastian Stan Knows ‘Absolutely Nothing’ About What Happens in the Movie
articles.summary: Directors Anthony and Joe Russo keeping the complete script from the cast, as with previous Avengers projects.
articles.body:
Long-time Marvel Winter Soldier star Sebastian Stan has clarified he knows nothing about the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, as he worked on the film without ever reading the complete script.

“I know absolutely nothing about it,” said Stan in a newly published French-language interview with French Sunday newspaper Le Journal du Dimanche . “Because we didn’t have a script. We just shot scattered scenes. It’s another way of working, continuously, constantly evolving. The producers didn’t want us to read it in its entirety, to avoid journalists asking us questions. I’ve been following this rule for fifteen years, I’m used to it.”

Stan’s comments came alongside a passing reference to The Batman: Part II being another project he can’t speak about. It’s been subsequently reported Le Journal du Dimanche’s article misquoted Stan making a reference to his role in the film, and the article has since been updated.

It’s worth noting the fact Stan hasn’t seen the complete Avengers: Doomsday script, despite being a part of the film, is actually par for the course when it comes to Marvel’s tentpole ensemble blockbusters.

While specifics vary slightly, it’s been previously reported that only Robert Downey, Jr. and Chris Evans received a full script for Avengers: Infinity War – although Benedict Cumberbatch also noted at the time that he too had read the complete script.

In an oral history of Avengers: Infinity War & Endgame with Rotten Tomatoes , the Russos admitted that only one actor definitely saw the complete script for Endgame: Robert Downey, Jr.

In Stan’s words, being able to participate in projects of such magnitude while still retaining the ability to watch it later as a spectator is part of the “beauty of this job.”

It sounds like he’ll be spectating it alongside a lot of other people, though, with Avengers: Doomsday pre-sale tickets reportedly outpacing Spider-Man: Brand New Day .

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: Fast Forever Starts Shooting in December, Confirms Vin Diesel
articles.summary: The supposedly final chapter in the Fast & Furious saga should begin shooting before the year is out.
articles.body:
The Fast & Furious saga’s leading man Vin Diesel has revealed that Fast & Furious 11 – officially known as Fast Forever – will begin shooting this December.

“We start shooting in December, if I can make good on the request from the studio,” Diesel told Variety ahead of a 25th anniversary screening of 2001’s The Fast and the Furious. “I’m in a good place, though. I’ve had to go through four sets of writers, four years of development, to get to something that I felt would be worthy of a finale.”

Diesel shared further details inside the screening itself, noting that after he read the complete script they had “worked so hard to make right,” he was crying.

“I couldn’t hold it back, and I had to tell everyone,” said Diesel. “And my sister said, ‘No more crying, bro.’ So I just want to say that sometimes, even the toughest guys in the world need to cry.”

While a video message from Vin Diesel published in July in costume as Dominic Torreto – and standing in front of the character’s iconic black 1970 Dodge Charger R/T – appeared to suggest production was already officially underway on Fast Forever, it later came to pass that the shoot was related to a World Cup promo that aired in the US during the US vs. Belgium game.

Fast Forever, the long-delayed and supposedly final chapter in the Fast & Furious film saga, is scheduled to hit cinemas on Friday, March 17, 2028. The release date and final title was announced by Universal earlier this year. However, little other information is actually known about the project, which still has no confirmed complete cast yet.

articles.title: The Pixel 11 isn’t the best Pixel of 2026, but it’s the smartest buy
articles.summary: Our review of the standard Google Pixel 11 is here. It’s easier to recommend than the 11 Pro, so long as superior image quality isn’t a top priority.
articles.body: It’d be easy to overlook the Pixel 11. Want the best cameras? The Pixel 11 Pro is your answer. Want the best bargain? The Pixel 10A is still a great deal. But the Pixel 11 might be the sweet spot in Google’s lineup this year. With 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, it delivers the same performance as the base Pixel 11 Pro for $899 — $200 less. And while it’s $400 more than the Pixel 10A, it has a faster processor, more RAM and storage, Qi2 charging, and a telephoto lens. It’s also the cheapest way to experience what’s actually new about the Pixel 11 series. With the hardware basically unchanged from the Pixel 10 except for new colors and a thinner camera bar, the spotlight this year has shifted to software, specifically features that aim to take full advantage of what most Pixel fans like about their phones: the cameras and special features that make the phones just a bit more helpful. Last year, we said Google’s Pixel 10 was priced fairly at $799, and that it’d be greedy for buyers to expect more from it. Well, RAMageddon happened, and everyone’s prices went up. The new Pixel 11 starts at $899 and has mostly the same specs. It adds a few exclusive software features that mostly make up for it and doubles the base storage. I guess it’d be greedy to expect much more from this one, too. [Product: Google Pixel 11 | https://www.amazon.com/Google-Pixel-11-Frost-Amazon/dp/B0HBF7RD17?tag=theverge02-20, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/8836598/type/dlg/https://store.google.com/us/product/pixel_11?hl=en-US, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fgoogle-pixel-11-256gb-unlocked-obsidian%2FJ39TC82XS9%2Fsku%2F6684444] The Pixel 11 looks, feels, and performs similarly to the $1,099 11 Pro. The Pro has a brighter, higher-resolution screen and much more powerful ultrawide and telephoto cameras, but the 11 is just as good in nearly every other way. It has the same Tensor G6 processor, and it even has the same amount of RAM as the base model Pro phone (though the more expensive Pro configurations have 16GB). In day-to-day use, I didn’t notice any performance issues owing to the smaller amount of RAM on the 11, though it’s possible that the newer processor balanced it out. Google didn’t hold back any of the software features from this model, either. As someone who doesn’t upgrade their phone unless they have to (I’m still very happy with my Pixel 9 Pro), I was skeptical that some of the phones’ most intriguing new camera features — Camera Looks and Magic Capture — would be enough to tempt me. Unfortunately for those like me who are holding off on upgrading for as long as possible, both features are rad. Like last year, the 11 has a 48MP main camera, 13MP ultrawide, and 10.8MP 5x telephoto, all of which are smaller and lower resolution than the sensors on the Pro phones. My Pixel 9 Pro’s wide and ultrawide lenses are roughly on par with the 11 Pro’s, and quite a bit more capable than the Pixel 11’s. But in the past week of testing, I don’t miss them as much as I thought I would. Camera Looks in particular helped me have more fun shooting with a Pixel than I have in years. It’s satisfying to quickly swap between different sensor-level presets, and they can make a big impact on how a photo turns out. [Image: The Pixel 11 is fast enough to snag not just a good photo of a Spider-Man imposter on the Brooklyn Bridge while driving by in a car, but a great one. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/PXL_20260813_210704991.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I’ve been a Pixel user since 2017, going from the 2 to the 3 to the 6 to the 9 Pro, almost entirely because of the cameras. I trust them to take great shots quickly and with little effort. I even brought the Pixel 2 on my honeymoon trip instead of a DSLR, and no, I don’t regret it all these years later. If you’re a serious phone photographer who spends time composing every shot, you’ll probably want to go for the Pro, but for more casual photographers like me, the quality difference isn’t that noticeable, especially with Camera Looks applied. Camera Looks has even encouraged me to slow down sometimes to put a little more effort into my composition. Camera Looks seems like Google’s realization that the Pixel’s default vibrant HDR-drenched look isn’t the best choice for every photo. Now, it’s easy to switch to the bold, slightly more muted “Digi” or the black-and-white “Black Tie” styles when you want to take a more impactful photo. If you like one of the looks enough to make it your default shooting style, you can lock it in. And it’s easier to make adjustments on the fly, thanks to the new quick access dials you can pin to the viewfinder. You can add dials for exposure, color temperature, and shadows. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/velvet.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/classic.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/digi.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/blacktie.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/minimal.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/default.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Magic Capture — another camera feature exclusive to the 11 series — is genuinely useful. The hybrid camera mode records a video and intelligently plucks hi-res photos and video clips from it, and I used it to capture a bunch of little moments with our two-year-old at the beach and at parks. It’s convenient to have a setting that can capture the unexpected without missing a beat. You can also manually capture photos while it’s recording. However, the photos are the highlight, not the video. (The resulting video looks choppier than a standard video, as if it lacks image stabilization; it doesn’t seem like it’s meant for consumption.) I’m more the type who’d like to shoot individual photos, as it feels great to happen upon a spectacular shot. But the AI does a good enough job at capturing little moments in the action. [Image: The Pixel 11’s camera bar is a little thinner than before, and Google’s new Pixelsnap case makes it sit flat on a table. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268705_Pixel_11_review_CFAULKNER_P1011489.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Another new software component available only on the Pixel 11 lineup is Gemini’s Proactive Assistance feature. It’s meant to handle more of the grunt work of using a phone for things like managing calendars, making reservations, and buying groceries. To actually have it do things for you, you need to give the agentic AI permission (it’s not on by default) to make changes within an array of apps, ranging from Google’s productivity suite to apps like OpenTable, Instacart, Google Messages, and more. It’s partially helpful, but like an intern that gets just enough wrong that you just feel better doing it yourself. In my back-and-forth text-a-thon with David Imel, who reviewed the 11 Pro, Proactive Assistance was more miss than hit. One of the features Google advertises is an OpenTable integration that pops up a Gemini chip to book a restaurant reservation if it sees a relevant message. We could only get it to work by being as specific and formal as possible, including the restaurant’s full name and the specific day and time. That’s not how most people type to each other.  [Image: The Pixel 11’s screen resolution is equivalent to that of the Pixel 10 as well as the Pixel 10A. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268705_Pixel_11_review_CFAULKNER_P1011482.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Here’s another example of Proactive Assistance in action: I was able to order groceries through my grocery list in Google Keep, but only after I figured out some unstated rules. After I enabled access to both Google Keep and Instacart in Gemini’s settings, I had to adjust the title of my Google Keep list to include “Instacart” (so much for being able to use natural language). Afterward, the feature quickly connected me with a list of nearby retailers that could fulfill my order, just like it does in the Instacart app. Proactive Assistance is intriguing, but I hope it gets better. You can read more about the feature’s quirks in David’s review; for now, it’s not worth upgrading for.  [Image: Google’s latest Pixel looks similar to its predecessor, but that’s not a bad thing. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268705_Pixel_11_review_CFAULKNER_P1011477.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] When I bought the Pixel 9 Pro two years ago, I picked the Pro because it was much better. It had a telephoto camera, more RAM, and more special features than the standard model. And its price came in under $1,000. This year, that’s all changed. The standard Pixel 11 now has a telephoto lens and just as much RAM as the $1,099 Pro, it’ll get all the same software features, and it’s now the one with a price under four digits. If you’re serious about phone photography, the 11 Pro is probably worth it for the bigger camera sensors. However, as someone who bought the Pixel 9 Pro two years ago, the Pixel 11’s blend of good-enough hardware and compelling software feels Pro enough to me. Photography by Cameron Faulkner/ The Verge

It has the same Tensor G6 processor, and it even has the same amount of RAM as the base model Pro phone (though the more expensive Pro configurations have 16GB). In day-to-day use, I didn’t notice any performance issues owing to the smaller amount of RAM on the 11, though it’s possible that the newer processor balanced it out. Google didn’t hold back any of the software features from this model, either. As someone who doesn’t upgrade their phone unless they have to (I’m still very happy with my Pixel 9 Pro), I was skeptical that some of the phones’ most intriguing new camera features — Camera Looks and Magic Capture — would be enough to tempt me. Unfortunately for those like me who are holding off on upgrading for as long as possible, both features are rad. Like last year, the 11 has a 48MP main camera, 13MP ultrawide, and 10.8MP 5x telephoto, all of which are smaller and lower resolution than the sensors on the Pro phones. My Pixel 9 Pro’s wide and ultrawide lenses are roughly on par with the 11 Pro’s, and quite a bit more capable than the Pixel 11’s. But in the past week of testing, I don’t miss them as much as I thought I would. Camera Looks in particular helped me have more fun shooting with a Pixel than I have in years. It’s satisfying to quickly swap between different sensor-level presets, and they can make a big impact on how a photo turns out. [Image: The Pixel 11 is fast enough to snag not just a good photo of a Spider-Man imposter on the Brooklyn Bridge while driving by in a car, but a great one. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/PXL_20260813_210704991.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I’ve been a Pixel user since 2017, going from the 2 to the 3 to the 6 to the 9 Pro, almost entirely because of the cameras. I trust them to take great shots quickly and with little effort. I even brought the Pixel 2 on my honeymoon trip instead of a DSLR, and no, I don’t regret it all these years later. If you’re a serious phone photographer who spends time composing every shot, you’ll probably want to go for the Pro, but for more casual photographers like me, the quality difference isn’t that noticeable, especially with Camera Looks applied. Camera Looks has even encouraged me to slow down sometimes to put a little more effort into my composition. Camera Looks seems like Google’s realization that the Pixel’s default vibrant HDR-drenched look isn’t the best choice for every photo. Now, it’s easy to switch to the bold, slightly more muted “Digi” or the black-and-white “Black Tie” styles when you want to take a more impactful photo. If you like one of the looks enough to make it your default shooting style, you can lock it in. And it’s easier to make adjustments on the fly, thanks to the new quick access dials you can pin to the viewfinder. You can add dials for exposure, color temperature, and shadows. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/velvet.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/classic.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/digi.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/blacktie.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/minimal.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/default.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Magic Capture — another camera feature exclusive to the 11 series — is genuinely useful. The hybrid camera mode records a video and intelligently plucks hi-res photos and video clips from it, and I used it to capture a bunch of little moments with our two-year-old at the beach and at parks. It’s convenient to have a setting that can capture the unexpected without missing a beat. You can also manually capture photos while it’s recording. However, the photos are the highlight, not the video. (The resulting video looks choppier than a standard video, as if it lacks image stabilization; it doesn’t seem like it’s meant for consumption.) I’m more the type who’d like to shoot individual photos, as it feels great to happen upon a spectacular shot. But the AI does a good enough job at capturing little moments in the action. [Image: The Pixel 11’s camera bar is a little thinner than before, and Google’s new Pixelsnap case makes it sit flat on a table. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268705_Pixel_11_review_CFAULKNER_P1011489.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Another new software component available only on the Pixel 11 lineup is Gemini’s Proactive Assistance feature. It’s meant to handle more of the grunt work of using a phone for things like managing calendars, making reservations, and buying groceries. To actually have it do things for you, you need to give the agentic AI permission (it’s not on by default) to make changes within an array of apps, ranging from Google’s productivity suite to apps like OpenTable, Instacart, Google Messages, and more. It’s partially helpful, but like an intern that gets just enough wrong that you just feel better doing it yourself. In my back-and-forth text-a-thon with David Imel, who reviewed the 11 Pro, Proactive Assistance was more miss than hit. One of the features Google advertises is an OpenTable integration that pops up a Gemini chip to book a restaurant reservation if it sees a relevant message. We could only get it to work by being as specific and formal as possible, including the restaurant’s full name and the specific day and time. That’s not how most people type to each other.  [Image: The Pixel 11’s screen resolution is equivalent to that of the Pixel 10 as well as the Pixel 10A. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268705_Pixel_11_review_CFAULKNER_P1011482.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Here’s another example of Proactive Assistance in action: I was able to order groceries through my grocery list in Google Keep, but only after I figured out some unstated rules. After I enabled access to both Google Keep and Instacart in Gemini’s settings, I had to adjust the title of my Google Keep list to include “Instacart” (so much for being able to use natural language). Afterward, the feature quickly connected me with a list of nearby retailers that could fulfill my order, just like it does in the Instacart app. Proactive Assistance is intriguing, but I hope it gets better. You can read more about the feature’s quirks in David’s review; for now, it’s not worth upgrading for.  [Image: Google’s latest Pixel looks similar to its predecessor, but that’s not a bad thing. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268705_Pixel_11_review_CFAULKNER_P1011477.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] When I bought the Pixel 9 Pro two years ago, I picked the Pro because it was much better. It had a telephoto camera, more RAM, and more special features than the standard model. And its price came in under $1,000. This year, that’s all changed. The standard Pixel 11 now has a telephoto lens and just as much RAM as the $1,099 Pro, it’ll get all the same software features, and it’s now the one with a price under four digits. If you’re serious about phone photography, the 11 Pro is probably worth it for the bigger camera sensors. However, as someone who bought the Pixel 9 Pro two years ago, the Pixel 11’s blend of good-enough hardware and compelling software feels Pro enough to me. Photography by Cameron Faulkner/ The Verge

articles.title: Xbox Special Edition Translucent Green Controller Price, Release Date Leaked
articles.summary: Pricing and launch details for Microsoft's snazzy translucent green Xbox controller have leaked online.
articles.body:
Pricing and launch details for Microsoft's snazzy translucent green Xbox controller have leaked online.

Inspired by the iconic OG Xbox console, the Xbox Wireless Controller Special Edition X25 will launch on October 20, 2026 priced at $79.99 / £74.99 / €79.99, according to Dealabs ' ever-reliable billbil-kun.

Microsoft will reportedly make these details official next week at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany, with preorders set to go live on August 26. As yet, however, there's no word on the X25 Special Edition Xbox Series X — or at least, not word that has leaked.

The 25 Best Original Xbox Games of All Time

Xbox announced its limited-edition Xbox Series X console variant inspired by the original Xbox back in June, in celebration of the brand's 25th anniversary.

The console and controller both sport a translucent green shell, allowing you to see all of the inner-workings of the machine and its pad. As you might expect, the console will come bundled with a matching controller, as well as the pad being able to buy separately. The console itself is expected to launch sometime this November.

Xbox does not appear to be holding a dedicated press conference at Gamescom, but will hold two days of livestreams showing off its extensive slate of upcoming titles in detail. Expect a look at games such as Gears of War: E-Day, Minecraft Dungeons 2, and Fable on Wednesday, August 26. The following day, updates for Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, plus Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and much more will be discussed.

As for big new surprises... perhaps we'll see some pop up in the event's main Opening Night Live showcase? As ever, IGN will be reporting on that live next Tuesday, August 25.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Latest Xbox Console Updates Include Extremely Belated Profile Badge if You Bought an Xbox One Back in 2013
articles.summary: New Xbox console features include a special profile badge if you forked out for an Xbox One on day one back in November 2013.
articles.body:
New Xbox console features include a special profile badge if you forked out for an Xbox One on day one back in November 2013.

Microsoft has detailed its latest system updates coming to Xbox Series X/S consoles, including improvements to your home and game library screens, plus more control over your local game saves.

Perhaps most surprising is an extremely belated profile badge to owners of the Xbox One "Day One" achievement, which you could unlock by buying Microsoft's then-new console back in 2013. As someone who did indeed do this, I remember redeeming the product code on a piece of paper included in the box to get my 0 Gamerscore achievement that confirmed I had indeed purchased Microsoft's least beloved console generation. And now it is displayed on my Xbox profile, too!

This addition comes amid a refresh for profile badges in general, which now display high-resolution artwork and a description for each.

Perhaps more usefully, you can now further customize your Xbox's home screen by removing items from the recent games and apps list, including the Play History tile. There's a cool-looking immersive background mode, too, that you can enter via the R3 button on your controller. This effectively hides all Home UI elements, allowing your background to take center stage.

If you're looking to free up some hard drive space, another new option lets you browse your local game saves and remove any taking up too much room. They're all in the cloud, anyway! Removing local copies will tidy up hard drive space and just prompt a quick download of the cloud version the next time you load up your game.

Last but not least, purchased games will now be removed from your purchase wishlist. Handy!

All of these features will begin rolling out to Xbox owners today, though most will arrive slowly, and to Xbox Insiders first as they are bug-tested and approved for wider rollout.

Which are you most looking forward to? And are there any other Xbox One day one owners in the house?

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Former Tekken 8 Director Kohei Ikeda Joins VS Studio, Re-Teams With Tekken Veteran Katsuhiro Harada
articles.summary: The news likely won’t come as a surprise to hardcore fighting game fans.
articles.body:
Former Tekken 8 Director Kohei Ikeda has announced he has joined newly established developer VS Studio, the Tokyo-based, SNK-owned outfit that was founded in May 2026 by former Tekken producer and director Katsuhiro Harada.

“I’ve joined VS Studio as the next step in my journey,” confirmed Ikeda via social media. “Working on games again with two of my former bosses feels nostalgic in many ways, while at the same time, the excitement of creating something completely new makes every day incredibly fulfilling.”

“I’m really looking forward to seeing what we can create together!”

Ikeda left Namco Bandai back in June . His 20-year stint at the storied developer culminated with his duties as game director on both Tekken 7 and 8. At least according to Harada, Ikeda’s final direction on Tekken involved ensuring one of Harada’s own final requests came to fruition, which was his plan to tease the return of Roger Jr. by re-creating a 10-year-old viral clip out of Australia of a man punching a kangaroo to rescue a dog .

Ikeda’s exit came rapidly in the wake of Harada’s own departure following over three decades at Namco Bandai, after which the Tekken legend quickly founded VS Studio.

A glimpse at what VS Studio has in store is likely some way off, but it would appear there is no shortage of fighting game experience assembled at the new developer so far.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: YouTuber Named in Take-Two GTA 6 Leaker Subpoena Insists He Did Nothing Wrong
articles.summary: The YouTuber named in Take-Two's GTA 6 leaker subpoena has denied any wrongdoing.
articles.body:
The YouTuber named in Take-Two's GTA 6 leaker subpoena has denied any wrongdoing.

Today it emerged that Take-Two had issued a subpoena in a federal court requesting information from both Microsoft and Discord as it hunts the leaker or leakers behind the recent spate of GTA 6 gameplay videos.

First reported by Kotaku , the Rockstar Games parent company issued the request yesterday, August 20, in the New York Southern District Court as part of a Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) subpoena. It wants information and records relating to the ‘CyberLeek’ account, which is allegedly behind the GTA 6 leaks.

Every Detail in the GTA 6 Cover Art Explained

The subpoena requests identifying information associated with user accounts that were members of a number of Discord servers. One of the Discord servers mentioned in the filing is 'discord.gg/darkviperau,' which is described as the DarkViperAU editors' server. DarkViperAU is the online name of Australian GTA content creator Matthew "Matt" Judge, who has 2.27 million subscribers on YouTube and nearly 900,000 followers on Twitch. Judge has published detailed breakdowns of the leaked GTA 6 videos this week on his various channels.

In a tweet , Judge responded to Take-Two's subpoena and the mention of his name within it. "I don't know anything," he insisted. "That isn't my editors’ Discord. There aren't even any clips of the leaks in either of my Discords.

"I am confused. I did say he can't drive multiple times, so maybe I caused him to write 'Cyberleek can't drive' on the most recent clips? Maybe he visited my Discord, I dunno. Rockstar hasn't emailed me, I suspect if they thought I knew something personally they would do so.

"Everyone is talking about these leaks, I am not special, hopefully."

Judge then held a three-hour livestream across YouTube and Twitch titled, “TakeTwo Has Subpoenad [sic] My Discord To Look For Leaker (News),” to respond further. Clearly shocked at recent events, Judge joked: “Rockstar just murdered me. I got better though.”

Judge said he “accidentally” showed a screenshot of the latest leaked GTA 6 video on-stream, but he immediately took it down and deleted it “because I don’t want to get in trouble.”

While the GTA 6 leaks were discussed and may have even been shared in his Discord, Judge insisted he had nothing to do with how the videos hit the internet. "I don't know this leaker!" Judge said. "I have personally shared nothing... at least not intentionally."

Judge continued: "I'm hoping this is one hand not speaking to the other hand, kind of thing. As in, the people at Take-Two have no idea who I am and so subpoenaed this stuff not knowing anyone at Rockstar could have DMd me at any time, or emailed me. I have had dozens of conversations with people from Rockstar Games. If Rockstar was truly unhappy with something I was doing, I think they would have just emailed me. Or they would have emailed all of us, because we're all on a community email."

"This has been an interesting time,” he concluded. “I'm sure I'm gonna be fine, guys. This is weird, but I’ve done nothing wrong. No-one’s done anything wrong. It’s just interesting. Definitely one for the history books. One more thing to add to my very very long, strange career.

“And if the feds ask you stuff, don’t tell them anything,” he joked, once again. "Deny everything chat! Burn the evidence!"

"The copyrighted material includes but is not limited to audio visual content, artwork, images, dialogue, or other creative elements," the filing reads. "Take-Two, through its counsel of record, has submitted a sworn declaration confirming that the purpose for which the DMCA subpoena is sought is to obtain the identity of an alleged infringer or infringers, and that such information will only be used for the purpose of protecting Take-Two’s rights."

Neither Take-Two nor Rockstar have commented on the recent GTA 6 leaks , nor have the companies commented on the court filing. IGN has asked for comment.

The subpoena has emerged even as the leaker continues to release GTA 6 gameplay videos. Today, August 21, the GTA 6 leaks stretched into a fourth consecutive day after yet another gameplay video hit the internet. As with the previously released videos, it advertises a memecoin, which one GTA fan recently traced to a Seychelles-based cryptocurrency exchange that might be used to identify the leaker . The watermark on this latest video reads: "HIGHER MARKET CAP = MORE LEEKS."

The leaks come just a week before the release of Grand Theft Auto 6: An Extended Look , which is a timed Netflix exclusive. That’s due Thursday, August 27, and will remain exclusive on Netflix for six hours before it makes its way to other platforms such as YouTube.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.
